articles.title: Ryan Waldschmidt hits game-winning 2-run HR with 2 outs in 9th to send D-backs past Cubs 5-4
articles.summary: Pinch-hitter Ryan Waldschmidt hit a game-winning, two-run homer with two outs in the ninth inning and the Arizona Diamondbacks rallied to stun the Chicago Cu...
articles.body:
PHOENIX (AP) — Pinch-hitter Ryan Waldschmidt hit a game-winning, two-run homer with two outs in the ninth inning and the Arizona Diamondbacks rallied to stun the Chicago Cubs 5-4 on Tuesday night.

The D-backs pulled one game behind the San Diego Padres for the final NL wild-card spot.

Trailing 4-3 in the ninth, Tim Tawa coaxed a one-out walk from Jacob Webb to start the decisive rally. Ildemaro Vargas flew out to right field for the second out before pinch-runner Jose Fernandez stole second base. Waldschmidt — a rookie — then launched a no-doubt homer over the left field fence to set off a raucous celebration.

It was Waldschmidt's second walk-off homer of the season.

Arizona trailed 4-0 in the eighth before mounting a two-out rally against reliever Daniel Palencia . Gabriel Moreno hit a check swing RBI double that hugged the first base line and stayed fair before Geraldo Perdomo 's two-run single cut the deficit to 4-3. Webb relieved Palencia and coaxed a ground out from Max Kepler to end the threat.

Ian Happ hit a three-run homer in the fourth to push the Cubs ahead 3-0. Michael Busch 's RBI single in the sixth made it 4-0. Busch and Seiya Suzuki both had two hits.

The D-backs' rally ruined a great outing for Clay Holmes , who breezed through the D-backs' lineup, giving up two singles and two walks while striking out five over seven scoreless innings. The right-hander has given up just one earned run over his past 19 innings, spanning three starts.

Arizona's Brandon Pfaadt (7-2) gave up four runs on six hits and two walks, striking out three. He didn't allow a hit over the first three innings, but gave up a single and a double in the fourth before Happ's three-run homer.

The D-backs send LHP Eduardo Rodriguez (13-4, 2.61 ERA) to the mound to face Cubs LHP Matthew Boyd (8-2, 4.15).

articles.title: Scientists found a 4-million-year-old baby tapir in Spain, the most complete juvenile skeleton of its kind ever found in Europe
articles.summary: Europe News: At the Camp dels Ninots site in Caldes de Malavella, near Girona in northeastern Spain, researchers have recovered a remarkably complete skeleton of a.
articles.body: At the Camp dels Ninots site in Caldes de Malavella, near Girona in northeastern Spain, researchers have recovered a remarkably complete skeleton of a young tapir that died roughly 4 million years ago, when the region was still home to a humid subtropical landscape surrounding an ancient volcanic lake. The animal, estimated to have been about 1 year old, belongs to Tapirus arvernensis, an extinct species that lived across parts of Europe during the Pliocene. Its bones were found largely connected in their original anatomical positions, preserving an unusually detailed record of a juvenile animal that would otherwise be extremely difficult to study. Researchers from the Catalan Institute of Human Palaeoecology and Social Evolution, or IPHES-CERCA, say the specimen is the most complete juvenile tapir skeleton ever recovered in Europe. The discovery also brings the number of tapir individuals found at Camp dels Ninots to 7, making the site an exceptionally important record of this extinct European mammal.Why Camp dels Ninots has become a major site for studying ancient tapirsAccording to IPHES-CERCA, the Camp dels Ninots excavation has produced an unusually large number of Tapirus arvernensis remains, including individuals representing different ages and sexes. The newly recovered juvenile is particularly valuable because complete young skeletons are rare in the fossil record. Dr Bruno GÃ³mez de Soler, an IPHES-CERCA researcher and co-director of the excavation, said the find provides an opportunity to study skeletal development, growth and other aspects of early life that are difficult to reconstruct from isolated fossil bones. Having several individuals from the same species and site also gives researchers an unusual opportunity to compare animals at different stages of development rather than relying on specimens recovered from unrelated locations.How an ancient volcanic lake preserved the tapir skeletons so wellCamp dels Ninots formed within a volcanic crater known as a maar, which later filled with water and became a lake during the Pliocene. Fine sediments accumulated on the lake floor over time, creating conditions that could rapidly bury animal remains and protect them from the processes that normally destroy fossil skeletons. That helps explain why the site has yielded exceptionally well-preserved animals, including tapirs whose bones remain in close anatomical association. Researchers have proposed that volcanic activity and gases released around the crater may have contributed to sudden animal deaths, although the precise circumstances surrounding individual specimens remain an area of investigation. The surrounding environment was also very different from modern northeastern Spain, with plant remains indicating a warmer, wetter landscape and dense vegetation around the ancient lake.What the juvenile tapir can reveal about how the species grewThe juvenile skeleton gives researchers something adult specimens cannot: a direct record of a developing Tapirus arvernensis. Young animals are particularly difficult to preserve because their developing bones are more vulnerable to destruction, scattering and scavenging before burial. Because Camp dels Ninots has produced tapirs of different ages, researchers can compare skeletal features across the population and begin reconstructing how these animals changed as they matured. The specimen will undergo further laboratory analysis after excavation, including detailed recording of the bones and examination of the surrounding sediment. Researchers hope those studies will clarify aspects of the animal's development while also revealing more about the conditions that allowed its skeleton to survive for approximately 4 million years.Why 7 tapirs from one site matter to palaeontologistsThe latest discovery strengthens Camp dels Ninots' importance as a reference site for understanding Europe's Pliocene tapirs. Tapirus arvernensis was one of the tapir species that inhabited Europe before the animals eventually disappeared from the continent, leaving their modern relatives restricted mainly to Asia and the Americas. Finding multiple individuals from one exceptionally preserved environment allows researchers to study not only individual animals but also variation within a single population. The combination of adults and juveniles is especially significant because it provides a rare opportunity to investigate growth and life history using fossils from the same geological setting. Rather than being simply another isolated prehistoric skeleton, the newly recovered tapir adds another piece to an unusually detailed record of an extinct animal and the environment in which it lived.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Miami Hurricanes Sued by Former WR in Unusual Transfer Portal Twist
articles.summary: The Hurricanes face a lawsuit from former receiver Cam Vaughn with an unusually familiar transfer portal argument at its center. The post Miami Hurricanes Su...
articles.body:
The Miami Hurricanes have made the transfer portal one of the foundations of their roster-building under Mario Cristobal. Now, a former Miami wide receiver is taking the program to court over what he says is the school's refusal to let him use it.

Cam Vaughn filed a lawsuit against Miami and the NCAA on Aug. 25 seeking the ability to enter the transfer portal after the Hurricanes dismissed him from the football program on Aug. 17. Vaughn transferred to Miami from West Virginia in January.

Considering Miami's recent history with cornerback Xavier Lucas and quarterback Darian Mensah, Vaughn's dispute with the university makes this an intriguing development.

Cam Vaughn Lawsuit Targets Miami, NCAA Over Portal Access

On3's Alex Byington, citing reporting from Pete Nakos, reported that Vaughn's representatives filed the lawsuit in Miami-Dade County against the university and NCAA.

Vaughn's representative, Blake Sercye, said Miami canceled the receiver's scholarship and then declined to make the waiver request needed for him to enter the portal outside the normal transfer window.

"On August 17, 2026, Miami dismissed Cam and cancelled his scholarship with no written explanation, no identified rule violation, and no hearing. Miami then refused to submit the waiver request the NCAA requires so that he can enter the transfer portal — leaving Cam without the ability to pursue his education or a team to play for. We are asking the court to hold Miami and the NCAA responsible for their failures to Cam, and grant him the relief he needs so that he can continue his education and career," Sercye said.

Those are allegations made by Vaughn's representative. On3's report did not include a response from Miami.

Vaughn has logged 83 passes for 1,344 yards and nine touchdowns between Jacksonville State and West Virginia in the last three years.

Miami Benefited From Similar Portal Fights With Xavier Lucas, Darian Mensah

Miami's recruitment of Lucas and Mensah previously makes this entire situation a bit awkward.

A year before Vaughn's lawsuit, defensive back Xavier Lucas wanted to leave Wisconsin. The Miami Herald's Jordan McPherson reported the Badgers did not enter his name into the transfer portal after he submitted his paperwork, citing a two-year NIL agreement they maintained was binding.

Lucas publicly accused Wisconsin of impeding his ability to transfer. He eventually unenrolled from Wisconsin and enrolled at Miami in January 2025 without ever appearing in the portal.

Wisconsin later sued Miami in June 2025, alleging the Hurricanes had impermissibly contacted Lucas and induced him to break his agreement. Miami denied wrongdoing and moved to dismiss the lawsuit.

Miami found itself in another transfer fight in January 2026. The Miami Herald's Barry Jackson and Jordan McPherson reported Duke and quarterback Darian Mensah reached a settlement after the Blue Devils sued to keep him from leaving, arguing his multiyear NIL agreement remained enforceable. The settlement cleared Mensah to transfer , and he committed to Miami later that day.

The circumstances aren't identical. Wisconsin's fight with Lucas and Duke's with Mensah centered heavily on contractual obligations, while Vaughn's representatives are challenging what happened after Miami dismissed him and canceled his scholarship.

Still, the common thread is difficult to miss.

Twice in a little more than a year, Miami benefited when prominent players sought to leave schools that tried to restrict their movement. According to Vaughn's lawsuit, the Hurricanes are now refusing to take the administrative step he needs to pursue the same freedom elsewhere.

Whether Vaughn's legal claims succeed is for the court to decide. For a program that has been one of college football's most aggressive portal shoppers, simply being on this side of the dispute creates an unusually uncomfortable look.

articles.title: Kirb’ed: Mariners 4, Phillies 1
articles.summary: Stifled in Seattle
articles.body:
The offense continued to sputter to begin the road trip and wasted another encouraging effort from Aaron Nola as the Philadelphia Phillies (73-60) dropped their second straight against the Seattle Mariners (64-69) on Tuesday night.

Mariners' starter, George Kirby , kept the offense in check most of the night but allowed the first run of the game in the second inning as Bryson Stott , Brandon Marsh and Justin Crawford strung together a trio of one-out singles.

After registering his first three-homer game last night, Cal Raleigh tied the game with a solo shot to begin the bottom of the second for his fourth home run in as many at bats.

Nola conceded the tie in the bottom of the sixth on an RBI single by Josh Naylor following a one-out single and a steal by Julio Rodriguez .

Aside from the two runs on three hits and three walks, Nola looked to still be in command of his stuff entering the seventh inning with 92 pitches. Don Mattingly opted to give way to Orion Kerkering who, after getting a ground out to start the inning, loaded the bases on a hit by pitch, single and a walk. Kerkering induced a pop out by Randy Arozarena for the second out and Mattingly went to Brooks Raley to face the lefty, Dominic Canzone . Raley left a 1-1 sweeper over the plate that Canzone laced to left for a two-RBI single to effectively put the game away.

In Kerkering and Raley's defense, the offense had no answers for Kirby & Co. Kirby begrudging left the game two outs into the eighth after allowing a hit to Bryce Harper but the minor threat was quickly erased by Jose Ferrer on a Luis Arraez ground out.

articles.title: ‘That’s Your Job to Hate Them’ — Urban Meyer Issues No-Nonsense Take on Kyle Whittingham, Bryce Underwood Downplaying Ohio State Rivalry
articles.summary: Former coach Urban Meyer understands Kyle Whittingham’s point. He just thinks Michigan’s new head coach is approaching the Ohio State rivalry with a little t...
articles.body:
Former coach Urban Meyer understands Kyle Whittingham's point. He just thinks Michigan's new head coach is approaching the Ohio State rivalry with a little too much common sense.

After Whittingham rejected the idea that he needs to personally hate Ryan Day and Bryce Underwood called Ohio State "just another game," Meyer offered a very different philosophy. For the former Buckeyes coach, hatred does not have to be personal to be useful.

Urban Meyer Says Hatred Has a Place in The Game

During a recent The Triple Option podcast episode, Meyer said he never personally hated Jim Harbaugh or Brady Hoke, but that distinction disappeared once Michigan became the opponent.

"Do I hate them? Absolutely, I hate them, and that's your job to hate them," Meyer said. "You got to play the game."

Meyer predicted Whittingham may develop more of that edge after his first trip to Columbus as Michigan's head coach. More importantly, he argued that a coach at either program has to understand what the rivalry means to the people around it.

"You're not going to change that," Meyer said. "So play the game."

PREDICT THE CFB SEASON: PFN's Free CFB Playoff Predictor

Meyer then took the argument beyond rivalry theater. He said love, fear, and hate were the three greatest motivators he used when preparing his teams, and he deliberately tried to create situations that made his players angry before games.

"I wanted my team so angry coming out of that tunnel that they played with nastiness and violence to them," Meyer said.

There is some history behind the conviction. Meyer went 7-0 against Michigan during his seven seasons at Ohio State, never experiencing the rivalry from the losing locker room.

Bryce Underwood Adds Another Layer to Michigan's Approach

Whittingham's comments drew attention after he said a rivalry can be intense without a "hatred factor" and questioned whether hating Ohio State would improve Michigan's chances of winning.

Underwood then told NBC Sports' John Fanta in an original interview that the Buckeyes are "just another game, just guys in a different color."

Underwood will have a chance to test that approach again after a difficult first appearance in The Game. Ohio State beat Michigan 27-9 last November, with Underwood completing eight of 18 passes for 63 yards and an interception.

His freshman season still showed plenty of upside. Underwood finished with a 78.0 PFSN QB Impact grade, ranking No. 79 nationally, while throwing for 2,428 yards and adding 392 rushing yards.

Michigan travels to Columbus on Nov. 28 for the 122nd meeting between the programs. Whittingham has made clear that he desperately wants to win it, even if he does not embrace the language surrounding it.

Meyer's message is simpler. In this rivalry, hatred is not supposed to describe the person across the field. It is supposed to help beat the colors they are wearing.

With Harris off the bubble and no longer on the roster, which Washington players need to shine during Wednesday's joint practice with the Ravens , followed by Friday's preseason finale?

With Jacory Croskey-Merritt and Jeremy McNichols battling injuries and Jerome Ford already gone, Henry has another chance to shine. The joint practice would allow defensive coordinator Daronte Jones to see Barber against stiffer competition.

Is the football world still waiting for Aaron Donald to decide whether he'll return from retirement for 2026, while another Donald-Rams workout has taken place at the Woodland Hills facility?

Aug 27, 2016; Denver , CO, USA; Los Angeles Rams defensive tackle Aaron Donald (99) during the second half of a preseason game against the Denver Broncos at Sports Authority Field at Mile High. The Broncos defeated the Rams 17-9.

The Los Angeles Rams are waiting on pins and needles for the possible return of the retired defensive star, who announced his retirement on social media in March 2024.

Talk of a comeback first gained traction after Donald admitted that the Rams' blockbuster trade for Myles Garrett got him thinking about whether that fire can light back up.

On Monday, Rams head coach Sean McVay gets honest about the team's plans and explained that the front office has plans for the alternative outcome.

"If he ends up doing it later, you could hypothetically–but that's not even part of our thought process," McVay told reporters . "Our thought process has been let's look at a 53 with him and a 53 not including him, and what does that look like?"

Donald worked out with the Rams for the second time on Aug. 16, and continues to put in work as he weighs a return to the NFL.

Dwight Freeney demands the real Aaron Donald

Former NFL edge Dwight Freeney says there's a difference between decent shape and football shape.

"If Aaron is Aaron… oh, it's gonna be a problem… It gotta be Aaron Donald as we remember, not just a guy with Aaron Donald's name."

Stafford, who played with and won a Super Bowl alongside Donald, said that the guy's an absolute monster in the weight room. The quarterback has so much respect for him.

"Whatever's right for Aaron is right for us," he said . "And if that's, 'Hey, I don't think I can do it,' Hey man, I appreciate it. Thanks for everything you always did, and then, giving it a rip and trying to see if you could do it again."

Rams roster decisions are looming as the regular-season opener against the San Francisco 49ers draws closer.

articles.title: Wojo: Tigers flash glimpses of future as playoff light fades
articles.summary: The Tigers aren’t looking ahead to the future, at least not officially, but on nights like this, there are glimpses of the big-picture goal.
articles.body:
Detroit — The Tigers aren't looking ahead to the future, at least not officially. The playoffs are almost out of sight, if not quite out of mind.

But on nights like this, there are glimpses, micro-views of the big-picture goal. The Tigers have played 11 rookies this season, and four of them were key in a much-needed 4-1 victory over Tampa Bay Tuesday night at Comerica Park. The starting pitcher, Jackson Jobe , is 24 but not a rookie. In only his fourth start in 14 months after Tommy John surgery, he expanded his arsenal, maintained his composure and took a step forward.

That's what it's about now for the Tigers (62-70), who snapped a six-game losing streak that just about squashed their faint playoff hopes. The A.L. remains muddled with mediocrity, so the Tigers are only four games out of the wild card, but trail six teams. Because they've defied ridiculous odds before, we're legally required to note their chances currently stand at 3.8%.

Yes, that's better than the 0.2% odds they overcame in 2024. But the chances of overcoming astronomical odds twice in three years have to be more astronomical. With 30 games left, there's no sense belaboring the obvious, not when the future is up now. We'll have ample opportunity to pick through all that was squandered, and the nasty mistakes that were made.

In the meantime, the Tigers' young talent is gathering expedited experience. There was rookie reliever Drew Sommers throwing 1.2 shutout innings to earn his first MLB victory and lower his ERA to 2.93. There was rookie Hao-Yu Lee lacing a two-out RBI single in the seventh to expand the lead to 4-1. There was Kevin McGonigle, playing flawless defense at third and short, the favorite to win A.L. Rookie of the Year.

And there was rookie centerfielder Max Clark slamming his second career home run — his first in Comerica Park — and racing around the bases so quickly, he almost ran up the back of runner Javy Báez.

"I completely blacked out, it was a really cool moment," Clark said. "I looked up and I could see (Báez's) number within touching distance. I started to panic and slowed down a little bit."

Clark, 21, runs as if trying make up for lost time, or trying to catch his best friend, McGonigle. Clark, the No. 3 overall pick in 2023, is hitting .247 with a .704 OPS, and already looks like a speedy mainstay in center field. He prides himself on his defense to the point he sounded fairly disgusted after he overran a hit by Liam Hicks in the fourth inning, leading to the Rays ' only run. Hicks was awarded a double, but even Clark knew it was an error.

"It took a weird hop, but it's unacceptable regardless," Clark said. "It's almost embarrassing to be completely honest."

Clark is honest and glib, a spark plug in every way. AJ Hinch loved that Clark was so annoyed by his misplay he turned into Mad Max.

"It fired me up that he's pissed," Hinch said. "He needs to make that play, and he's not gonna give himself any grace. That's the high standard we need. He plays a very fast center field. He's going to be really good because of that. He goes home with a learning lesson, and makes my job a little easier."

Lots of lessons are being learned by the Tigers, young and old. In the offseason, they'll need to show they grasped something. It starts with president of baseball operations Scott Harris, who will have to explain his signings and acquisitions — and lack thereof — and how the Tigers' offense and bullpen became so maddeningly inconsistent. The Tigers have ridden one of the craziest rollercoasters in memory, rising from 16 games under .500 to within a whiff of first place, and then down again. The latest rough stretch coincided with the loss of Riley Greene to a hamstring injury, with the Tigers 3-10 in his absence.

None of the rookies this season were around for the 2024 miracle, so they're just trying to navigate the daily grind. And even as the Tigers fall out of the playoff picture, there's valuable experience to be gained.

Jobe was so annoyed by his "godawful" change-up in his last rocky outing against the White Sox , he worked on ramping up his curveball velocity. He's healthy but still shaking off rust, and threw 86 pitches in 4.1 innings. He battled a potent lineup and a Rays team with the best record in the A.L., striking out four, walking three and escaping a base-loaded jam in the fourth when Tampa Bay took a 1-0 lead.

"I'm just figuring out what works, trying different things, making some changes when I can," said Jobe, the third overall pick in 2021. "Today the curveball was very big for me, something I've been struggling with. It kind of turned into a real weapon, in my opinion. It definitely felt like a momentum shifter, potentially. We still have a lot of good energy in this clubhouse, hopefully we can turn it around."

Potentially and hopefully are the salient words for the Tigers now. Potential is what the Tigers are hoping to cash in, if not now, soon. You see glimpses of the confidence that made Jobe such a touted prospect, along with his fastball that touches 100. You see a star in McGonigle. You also see holes on a roster that will require some veteran help.

We'll see one wayward piece of their past this weekend when Tarik Skubal comes to town with the Dodgers . Has that trade cost the Tigers in the short term? Of course. But when Hinch hears his young guys beating themselves up for miscues, vowing to get better, his mood brightens, ever so slightly.

"You gotta let them grow up," Hinch said. "Sometimes, at this level, at this time of year, and where our team is, it's hard to recognize that."

It's not hard to recognize the potential of the Tigers' young players. It's also not hard to recognize the current odds, and the reality of a season in which way too many opportunities were wasted.

articles.title: Donald Trump sends Saudi civil nuclear deal to Congress, keeps Israel normalisation as condition
articles.summary: US News: US President Donald Trumpâs administration has submitted a proposed civil nuclear cooperation agreement with Saudi Arabia to Congress for review, whil.
articles.body: US President Donald Trumpâs administration has submitted a proposed civil nuclear cooperation agreement with Saudi Arabia to Congress for review, while maintaining that the pact will only move forward if Riyadh agrees to normalise relations with Israel.The agreement was sent to Congress on Monday under the requirements of the US Atomic Energy Act, according to an administration official cited by Reuters.The Wall Street Journal first reported the formal submission.The agreement was signed last month in Washington by US energy secretary Chris Wright and Saudi energy minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman. It would allow US companies to play a central role in developing Saudi Arabiaâs civilian nuclear programme.A US administration official told Reuters that Trumpâs position had not changed and that the agreement would only take effect if Saudi Arabia joins the Abraham Accords, the US-brokered framework for normalising relations between Israel and Arab and Muslim-majority countries.Trump had linked the nuclear deal to normalisation shortly after the agreement was reached. On July 23, he said the civil nuclear deal would be approved but was âtotally subject to Saudi Arabia joining the very respected and successful Abraham Accordsâ.Congress gets 90 days to review nuclear pactUnder US law, Congress has 90 days while in session to review the agreement. Unless lawmakers pass a joint resolution rejecting it during that period, the pact can take effect without a separate vote by either chamber.According to AP, the submission was made to Capitol Hill on Monday.The proposed pact is expected to last 30 years. It would facilitate the development of Saudi Arabiaâs nuclear infrastructure using US technology, including AP1000 reactors.The project could involve US firms in the construction and development of the programme following a joint US-Saudi study.The agreement has also drawn scrutiny over nuclear non-proliferation. Some Democratic lawmakers and non-proliferation advocates have criticised the pact because it does not bar Saudi Arabia from enriching uranium or reprocessing nuclear waste, which can provide potential pathways towards producing nuclear weapons.The United Arab Emirates accepted restrictions on enrichment and reprocessing, known as the âgold standardâ, in its 2009 civil nuclear agreement with the US.The Trump administration has said the Saudi agreement contains the non-proliferation measures required under US law.Saudi-Israel normalisation remains key hurdleTrumpâs condition could complicate the agreementâs path forward because Saudi Arabia has maintained that it would only establish diplomatic relations with Israel if there is a clear and irreversible path towards Palestinian statehood.Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has rejected Palestinian statehood, saying it would be untenable for Israelâs security.The Abraham Accords, reached in 2020 and 2021, established diplomatic relations between Israel and the United Arab Emirates, Bahrain, Morocco and Sudan. Saudi Arabia has so far not joined the framework.Trumpâs administration has nevertheless continued to pursue an expansion of the accords, while Riyadh has maintained its position on Palestinian statehood.The proposed nuclear agreement has also faced criticism in the US over its potential implications for nuclear proliferation in West Asia.Henry Sokolski, head of the Nonproliferation Policy Education Centre, told Reuters that beginning the congressional review could allow the deal to proceed without some of the restrictions sought by its critics.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Who was the woman who placed her hands on President Murmuâs shoulders at the Padma Awards? Meet Hirbai Ibrahim Lobi, the Siddi social worker who changed more than 700 lives
articles.summary: A quiet moment from the 2023 Padma Awards continues to draw attention. As she received the Padma Shri from President Droupadi Murmu at Rashtrapati Bha.
articles.body: A quiet moment from the 2023 Padma Awards continues to draw attention. As she received the Padma Shri from President Droupadi Murmu at Rashtrapati Bhavan, social worker Hirbai Ibrahim Lobi did something that stood out amid the formality of the ceremony- she reached out and affectionately placed her hands on the Presidentâs shoulders.The gesture was warm and spontaneous, and captured something of Lobiâs personality: a woman who had spent much of her life working at the grassroots and speaking for a community that has often remained outside the national spotlight. But who was Hirbai Ibrahim Lobi?Hirbai Ibrahim Lobi was a social worker from Jambur village in Gujarat's Gir Somnath district and a prominent member of the Siddi community, a small African-origin community that has lived in parts of India for centuries.She dedicated much of her life to improving the lives of Siddi women and children, particularly through education, financial independence, employment and better farming practices. Her work eventually earned her the Padma Shri in 2023 for social work.Lobi's own childhood was far removed from privilege. She lost her parents at a young age and was raised by her grandmother. Hirbai was married at the age of 14. She did not receive formal education, yet education remained one of the central themes of her life's work.She learned from the radio- and passed that knowledge onOne of the most remarkable parts of Lobi's story is how she educated herself. Without access to formal schooling, she turned to the radio. Programmes about agriculture, government schemes and women's development became an informal classroom for her. She would listen, learn and then share what she had learnt with other women in her community.Her interest in organic farming, for instance, began after she heard about techniques for making organic fertilizer on the radio. She later used that knowledge in her own community.Her work was especially significant because many Siddi women in the area depended on cutting wood for their livelihoods, sometimes working in areas around the Gir forest. Lobi worked to help women find alternative sources of income and become financially independent.From opening bank accounts to creating employmentLobi's work was not limited to awareness campaigns. She helped Siddi women understand banking and savings, encouraged them to become economically independent and worked with social organisations to create employment opportunities. More than 700 women were reported to have benefited from her efforts.She also worked to improve children's access to education and helped establish balwadis, or early-childhood learning centres, in the community.In 2004, she founded the Mahila Vikas Foundation, which became an important part of her work towards women's empowerment. The governmentâs Padma citation also notes that she was associated with the Adivasi Mahila Sangh, also known as the Siddi Women's Federation.Her approach was simple: learn something useful and make sure others could benefit from it too.The Padma Awards ceremony in March 2023 produced another memorable moment involving Lobi. As she walked towards the stage to receive her award, she stopped near Prime Minister Narendra Modi, who was seated in the front row with other Union ministers. Rather than simply walking past, she spoke about what the honour meant to her community.She told him that her community had lived in the forests and often remained unnoticed, describing the Padma Shri as an honour they had never imagined receiving. PM Modi responded by bowing his head and greeting her with folded hands. The exchange was followed by applause from those present at the ceremony.And then came the moment with President MurmuAfter speaking to the Prime Minister, Lobi went on to receive the Padma Shri from President Droupadi Murmu. And the viral moment happened. Lobi affectionately placed her hands on Murmu's shoulders. Once the award was given to her by the President, she again happily placed her hands on President Murmuâs shoulder. Her happiness could be seen through her eyes.Lobi's gesture appeared to carry the warmth and informality of someone meeting another woman from a similar social world, rather than treating the occasion only as a formal exchange between an award recipient and the country's President.A life built around her communityHirbai Ibrahim Lobi died at her home in Jambur village on January 24, 2025, at the age of 65. She was survived by two sons and a daughter. Her death was mourned as a major loss for the Siddi community.Looking for trusted parenting advice? articles.title: Brevard HEAT's dynamic offense leads to sweep of Melbourne CC
articles.summary: After both teams won all their first-week matches, Brevard HEAT showed its potential with a sweep of Melbourne Central Catholic to go to 4-0.
articles.body:
Melbourne Central Catholic traveled to Palm Bay on Aug. 25 to play Brevard HEAT in a matchup featuring undefeated teams.

Brevard HEAT's strong serving and balanced attack propelled the Firehawks to the sweep 25-12, 25-18, 25-16.

"Our first set was really strong," Brevard HEAT head coach Darrah Bowen said. "We struggled a little bit set two and three and just played.

The Firehawks ended the match with 26 kills and 14 aces. Senior Aine Hanley led the attack with 6 kills and 3 aces. Senior setter Anna Livengood comprised nearly have of the service aces with 6 to go with 2 kills. Sophomore Charis Bennett and senior Brooke Arce recorded 6 and 5 kills, respectively.

"We really work hard to make our serve an offensive weapon instead of just getting it over and it showed," Bowen said.

Firehawks take down Hustlers in girls volleyball

Livengood's presence was felt all over the court. The senior setter recorded a pair of dump kills in the first set. In set two, Livengood served 3 aces in 4 points fueling an 11-4 run to close out the second set.

"Just my coach, my teammates staying behind me after I missed my first serve," Livengood said. "My coach and my teammates said serve it this time. We're here to back you up. Them pushing me instead of being angry with me led me to get those aces."

Livengood, who dished out 52 assists through the first three games, is still building chemistry with the new players on the floor following graduations and transfers. She led the team with 680 assists last season.

"Coming into this season, we have a lot of key pieces missing. We have a couple girls that went and played college so just missing them this year," Livengood said. "We've had a couple girls come in transferring. A lot of new pieces we weren't really expecting that really came in and helped make this team what it is now."

Bowen coaches Hanley during the club season. The senior, who recorded 128 kills last season, has embraced playing back row this season and has become a productive defender with 40 digs through the first three games.

"(Hanley) came into the (club) team where she had to learn to be a leader. She embraced it and became the strongest player we had. This year, she just rolled with that," Bowen said. "She wasn't quite sure coming in what she looked like as an outside because she set for us the last couple years. She has just owned that back row, she talks loud, she encourages everyone. I don't want to take her off the court."

Brevard HEAT improved to 4-0 with its third-straight sweep after defeating Space Coast in 4 sets in the opener.

"I think we got a pretty solid group," Livengood said. "I think we're going to go pretty far in districts, regionals. I think as long as we come and reach our potential, I think we could go pretty far."

The Firehawks head to Merritt Island Christian on Aug. 27 before a regional final rematch with St. Edward's on Aug. 28. Bowen said she believes the team is well positioned to reach the state semifinals for the second time in 3 years.

"We've got a little more depth just from our front row and our back row where we didn't have that last year," Bowen said. "When we were missing a player, we were stuck. This year we actually have some height and it's going to make a difference."

Errors plagued Melbourne Central Catholic in its first defeat of the season. The Hustlers ended the game with 32 attacking and service errors to go with 14 kills and 5 aces.

"It wasn't our best. I just think we underestimated our competition after winning a few games in a row," Melbourne Central Catholic head coach Jessica McGuire said. "When the atmosphere is different, ceiling's lower and the court is shorter, it's easier to get rattled. We had our good moments, but we need to be more consistent."

MCC senior Catalina Mendoza led the team with 6 kills and 2 aces. Junior Rossi Deane chipped in with 5 kills.

In the back row, senior Emma Martin has anchored Hustlers defense. Martin dug a team-high 27 balls raising her total to 66 through four matches.

"(Martin's) been great," McGuire said. "Lots of awesome digs and usually amazing passes as well. She's really great and talkative and a good senior leader on our team."

In McGuire's first season, MCC began the season 2-0 for the first time since 2015. The Hustlers swept Cocoa Beach and defeated Titusville in five sets. The fast start, McGuire said, injected confidence into the squad.

"That was awesome. It was tough and that set the tone. We had our best setter get injured. She tore her ACL and we were able to pull off that game," McGuire said. "We beat Cocoa Beach and Titusville and they were all crying at the end. They hadn't beaten them additionally with a whole new lineup."

Melbourne Central Catholic hosts West Shore on Aug. 26 and Edgewood on Aug. 27. In search for its first winning season since 2014, McGuire said she believes the team is capable of turning heads this season.

"We are trying to win at least 75% of our games," McGuire said. "I think they only won 30% last year and I hope it's higher and we're ending up first or second in our district tournament and to go far. I think they have the capability. They just have to believe it because they've come from like 12 years of losing seasons."

Odyssey Charter def. Halifax Academy 3-0 (25-16, 25-12, 25-11)

Odyssey Charter swept Halifax Academy in its season opener behind 27 kills and 23 aces. Senior Lily Gilmore recorded 6 kills and a team-high 6 aces. Freshman Karigan Ford-Torres spiked a team-high 8 kills to go with 5 aces. Senior Lauren Janesky tallied 20 assists and 5 aces.

The Titans begin the year 1-0 and they'll head to Pineapple Cove Palm Bay on Aug. 27.

Edgewood def. Rockledge 3-0 (25-18, 25-19, 25-13)

The Red Wolves picked up their second sweep of the season as sophomore Maya Ferguson led the attack with 9 kills and 7 aces. They finished with 26 kills and 18 aces as a team.

Junior Adison Carter posted a double-double of 15 assists and 10 digs. Junior Kelsey Kennedy and senior Macy Ferguson spiked 7 and 5 kills, respectively.

Edgewood improved to 3-1 and it'll play back-to-back road games at Space Coast on Aug. 26 and Melbourne Central Catholic on Aug. 27. Rockledge fell to 0-4 and it'll host Eau Gallie on Sept. 1.

Viera def. Holy Trinity 3-0 (28-26, 27-25. 25-20)

In a hotly contested match, Viera picks up its second home win in a row with a sweep of Holy Trinity.

The Hawks moved to 3-0 and will head to Astronaut on Aug. 27. The Tigers lost their second game in a row and will bring a 1-2 record into their next match versus Vero Beach on Aug. 26 before heading to Orangewood Christian on Aug. 27.

Merritt Island def. New Smyrna Beach 3-0 (25-21, 25-19, 25-10)

The Mustangs finished with three attackers in double-figure kills. Junior Ema Michell recorded a dozen kills with junior Lydia Scott and senior Bella Becker finishing with 11 kills each.

Michell and senior Amber Ives served 4 aces. Scott blocked 4 shots with Michell, Becker and junior Peyton Riordan ending the match with 3 blocks each. Ives completed the night with 19 assists.

Merritt Island heads into a big weekend with a 4-0 record. The Mustangs play back-to-back road games against state finalists in defending Class 3A champion Calvary Christian Clearwater on Aug. 28 and Class 2A runner-up First Baptist Academy on Aug. 29.

Bayside def. Cocoa 3-0 (25-16, 25-11, 25-2)

Bayside entered the win column for the first time this season sweeping Cocoa at home.

The Bears improve to 1-2 and they'll play at Cocoa Beach on Aug. 27. The Tigers drop to 0-2 and will host the Minutemen on Aug. 26 before heading to Palm Bay on Aug. 27.

Melbourne def. Cocoa Beach 3-0 (25-19, 25-8, 25-13)

Melbourne earned the sweep in its home opener. The Bulldogs went 3-2 in the SSAA Invitational on Aug. 21-22 earning wins over Geneva Classical Academy, Evangelical Christian and Cambridge Christian. Melbourne lost to Lakewood Ranch and Southland Christian.

The Bulldogs moved to 5-3 and they'll play at Heritage on Aug. 27.

Satellite def. Titusville 3-0 (25-11, 25-19, 25-18)

The Scorpions won their third straight match in a game featuring state playoff teams from a year ago.

Titusville senior Hayden Thibert led the team with 10 kills. Sophomore Natalie Regan recorded 8 kills and a team-high 6 aces. Seniors Zoe Silva and Paisley Perry recorded double-figures assists with 14 and 12, respectively.

Satellite takes a 3-1 record into its next match at Merritt Island on Sept. 1. Titusville brings a 1-3 record into its next match versus Space Coast on Aug. 27.

Space Coast def. Eau Gallie 3-0 (25-5, 25-13, 25-13)

The Vipers spoil the season and home opener for Eau Gallie with a convincing sweep. They improve to 3-1 and they'll face Edgewood on Aug. 26 and Titusville on Aug. 27.

Eau Gallie starts the season 0-1 and it'll head to West Shore on Aug. 27.

articles.title: Holy Waldschmidt! Dbacks 5, Cubs 4
articles.summary: Mark Grace perhaps said it best in the postgame show when he said, “Im not sure we have seen a more unlikely Dbacks win the season” The almost Dback Clay Hol...
articles.body:
Mark Grace perhaps said it best in the postgame show when he said, "Im not sure we have seen a more unlikely Dbacks win the season"

The almost Dback Clay Holmes shut this Dbacks offense down for 7 innings. The Dbacks had a deal in place for Holmes per multiple reports but the deal fell through at the last minute due to medicals. The fact that he was almost a Dback made the first 7 innings of this game sting all that much more, especially given the current status of this rotation.

Brandon Pfaadt was pretty good today pitching into the 7 th inning tonight and allowing 4 runs while keeping his team within striking distance. The Cubs have the 2 nd best offense in the league and Pfaadt did a decent enough job of keeping them in check. His first 3 innings were pretty easy getting lots of soft contact, however he gave up a 3 run HR in the 4 th inning on a hanging curveball to Ian Happ . Most importantly however, like I mentioned earlier, he was able to settle back in after the home run and give his team 6.2 innings against a red hot offense.

The Dbacks offense finally woke up in the 8 th inning as they were able to finally get on the board with 3 runs due to some linked up at bats with a couple of walks and a huge double from the red hot Gabi Moreno and a single from Geraldo Perdomo . When this offense has been clicking this season, it seems as though it is starting with the bottom of the order getting on base for the top of the order.

The story of the game however was Ryan Waldsschmidt who for the second time this season hit a walkoff home run off of a contending team's closer. This time it came as a pinch hitter with 2 outs in the bottom of the 9 th with Jose Fernandez pinch running at first base for Tim Tawa . The Dbacks were inches away from losing this game as Jose Fernandez was narrowly able to steal 2 nd base and get into scoring position down 4-3. Then Waldschmidt got a hanging slider and did not miss it! What an electric moment and perhaps the biggest swing of the season thus far considering that the Dbacks were able to gain a game on both the Padres and the Phillies tonight on 1 single swing. What a great moment for this team!

The Dbacks will look to win the series tomorrow night and in the postgame interview Torey Lovullo insisted that Jordan Lawlar will be in the lineup tomorrow which is tremendous news for this team and for a guy that has had such unfortunate injury luck in his early career. So all is right in the desert tonight and what a tremendous boost for this team as the Dbacks will go into tomorrow 1 game out of a wild card spot!

articles.title: Practical Magic 2's Kidman and Bullock board Essex vintage train
articles.summary: The stars appear on the train, specially transported to a film studos for a new movie sequel.
articles.body:
A call from Hollywood producers asking if film stars Nicole Kidman and Sandra Bullock could sit in a vintage railway carriage came out of the blue for station manager Robert Bentley.

They called him to ask if the duo could use it for their new blockbuster, Practical Magic 2, a sequel to the 1998 romantic fantasy tale.

While film producers were keen to feature it, they first needed the train moved from North Weald, Essex, to the Warner Bros Studios in Leavesden, Hertfordshire.

The studio filming left Bentley "in awe", he said. "When you're stood at the studio and then all of a sudden Sandra is stood next to you, it's hard to describe the feeling."

The 27-year-old said he ended up chatting to Bullock, who was interested in the history of the train.

Epping Ongar Railway has preserved its stations and carriages since closing in the 1990s.

Its authentic appearance has made it a popular go-to spot for film-makers, with it appearing in the TV shows Man vs Baby and Death in Paradise in recent times.

Bentley said producers had scouted around for locations before choosing to use North Weald station for a scene with US actress Joey King, as well as its train carriage, for filming last summer.

The final choice for Bullock's scene was a 1960s British Rail Mark 1 coach.

"We were the perfect fit for them in terms of what they wanted to film," said Bentley.

"We had the countryside and we had the coach that they wanted."

He said payment was not six digits, but "quite a high figure".

The film-makers also asked him to stick around for a scene, casting him as the train guard with a line of dialogue.

Other scenes were filmed at St Mary and All Saints Church in Lambourne, near Abridge.

The Grade I-listed church dates back to the 12th Century, but producers felt it could pass for a US church.

Last year, it was reported film and TV shows being made in Essex generated £3m for the local economy since 2022.

The Daniel Craig thriller Wake Up Dead Man: A Knives Out Mystery - filmed at a church in Epping Forest - has been among the productions providing a boost.

Essex County Council established the Essex Film Office in 2022 to attract more large film productions to the county.

It provides a point of contact for production companies looking for perfect filming locations - guiding them in the right direction and assisting them with permissions.

Manager Erica Gilson recalled feeling "hugely proud" to work on Mr Bates vs The Post Office, which included scenes at Shire Hall in Chelmsford.

She was emotional as she spoke about the impact it had.

"You're a tiny, tiny part in something that ends up having a huge difference, and that's the power of the arts," she said.

Jeff Bray, the council's cabinet member for regeneration, planning and heritage, said the county has "so much to offer" film studios.

"We've got everything: wide open countryside, fantastic beaches, heritage of every kind from Roman through to Medieval - whatever you want you'll find it here in Essex," he said.

articles.title: 'I'm still paying a mortgage for a home destroyed by a fire'
articles.summary: Sarah Williams's flat was destroyed in a fire two years ago. Why is she still paying a mortgage on it?
articles.body:
Sarah Williams vividly remembers watching her home burn down on the news. On 26 August 2024, she was on holiday when a neighbour texted her to say the Spectrum Building in east London was on fire.

But two years on from the blaze in Dagenham, which left more than 80 people homeless, residents including Williams say they are still "in limbo".

The leaseholder said: "We're still just stuck waiting for other people to make decisions about our future."

She added that in a year's time, the money they were given through insurance to pay for alternative accommodation will run out, and she is still paying her mortgage for a home that does not exist.

At the time of the blaze, from which at least 20 people were rescued, work was under way to remove dangerous cladding. An investigation found the scaffolding around the building at the time had caused the fire to spread, although the exact cause of the blaze is unknown.

The government had provided almost £6m through its Building Safety fund to remediate the building - administered by the Greater London Authority (GLA) – with a clause stating that if the work was not completed, the money would have to be repaid.

The Spectrum Building was demolished in December 2024 after surveyor reports deemed it unsafe.

The building's freeholder, Arinium Ltd, has since gone into administration, leaving the administrators, FRP, in control of the company's assets, including the insurance proceeds.

The government says the GLA has told the building's administrators that the GLA may be owed money as part of the insolvency process.

The government says this is a standard procedural step and would not affect the money residents are owed, as the GLA would only receive any funds left after residents had been fully compensated.

The GLA said that, as is standard practice in insolvency law, it had informed the administrators of the government's interest as a potential creditor.

In the meantime, Williams is paying a mortgage of £750, and hopes to receive a payout from administrators to help pay it off.

But because of the insolvency dispute, she is still waiting for answers.

"I'm not cross at my mortgage provider for making me continue to pay the mortgage," Williams says. "They've been really supportive, and sympathetic when I've spoken to them on the phone," adding: "It just shows that the whole thing can collapse, right?

"Building insurance becomes absolutely useless because there wasn't enough to rebuild the building."

Williams blames the freeholder for underinsuring the building.

"There are no checks and balances to make sure what happened at Spectrum doesn't happen again."

James Allchurch was a leaseholder in a third-floor flat in the Spectrum Building. He told BBC London he "still has nightmares" about the night of the fire.

Recalling the fire in the early hours, he said: "We saw a load of flashing blue lights and embers floating down outside the window. The smell of burning hit me hard. We just threw on any old clothes and legged it out of the building as quickly as we could.

"We were among the last people to evacuate and it was surreal, looking at the burning building."

Since the fire, Allchurch said the freeholder of the building had been "nowhere to be seen" and described the situation as "poor".

"What we would like to see is lessons learnt. We'd like to see accountability and responsibility.

"There were belongings in that building that I can never recover - things that don't have a monetary value. Photos of my parents, an old watch that my dad left me. They can't be replaced. It's heartbreaking, and it'll take a long time to get over."

He says his experience has also raised wider concerns about fire safety and cladding.

In the time since, prompted by the Grenfell fire, the government has established a Building Safety Regulator, which is responsible for overseeing the safety and design of high-rise buildings across England, nearly 70% of which are in London.

At the time of the fire, the then deputy prime minister Angela Rayner visited the site of the blaze, and said there had been "slow progress" since the fire in Grenfell Tower and there was "still far too much cladding".

She added that it was important for residents to know that the government and the council "would be there for them".

But Williams says the words have been "followed by nothing".

She said she hoped Andy Burnham would "live up to the promises and the statements that he made when he was Manchester mayor", when he stood alongside cladding action groups and said: "This is not good enough."

Flats demolished due to safety concerns after fire

'Flying flaming objects' helped spread fire - LFB

Steve Dudeney, director of fire safety consultancy Ignis Fire and Resilience Ltd, and a former London Fire Brigade commander, said there had been "lots of talking and very little doing".

"It just seems bizarre. When it was in the media the government were making all the right noises, but two years on, people are still left in the lurch.

"People are still paying mortgages on what is effectively a pile of rubble. Where is the oversight?"

He says insurance money should be paid to those who are owed it.

"The fact that this hasn't been solved clearly points out that this is a massive problem."

Speaking about cladding remediation, he says there has been little change within the industry.

"In the industry, I don't see many changes. I see confusion, and cladding is still not being taken seriously.

"The landscape, for me, is as confusing as it was post-Grenfell. The bureaucratic process is an ongoing nightmare."

A spokesperson for the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government said: "The residents of the Spectrum Building must be fully and urgently compensated so they can start to rebuild their lives.

"We urge the building's administrators to resolve the insurance settlements quickly, and more broadly we continue to work to speed up cladding removal and bring the building safety crisis to an end."

The building's administrators FRP said in a statement: "We recognise how difficult the situation remains for former residents. We are in regular dialogue with resident groups throughout this process.

"This has been an incredibly complex case, demanding independent legal expertise and bespoke valuation models to assess the many individual claims.

"I'm pleased to say we are now applying to the court to approve the first round of payments to leaseholders and creditors. Getting money out to residents as quickly as the process allows is our priority."

A spokesperson for London Mayor Sir Sadiq Khan said: "Following the devastating fire at the Spectrum Building, the mayor has always been clear that the former residents must rightly and urgently be compensated for their losses.

"It is the responsibility of the Spectrum administrators to pay the funds to former residents to cover losses and damages caused by the fire."

The freeholder of the block, Arinium Ltd, has been approached for comment, but has not responded to the BBC.

articles.title: Kettering's Alfred East Art Gallery set to welcome visitors again
articles.summary: The Alfred East Art Gallery has been closed to the public for more than five years.
articles.body:
An art gallery will welcome visitors for the first time in more than five years by displaying a collection of work by local artists.

The Alfred East Art Gallery in Kettering, Northamptonshire, closed to the public in mid-2021 for redevelopment and later required extensive roof repairs following rain damage in 2023.

The gallery is part of a cultural hub, collectively known as Cornerstone, which also includes its library, museum and garden.

North Northamptonshire Council said that the new display, titled Prelude, would be located within the rear extension of the building from 5 September to 2 October ahead of the full reopening to coincide with Northamptonshire Day.

It will be the first exhibition to feature in the new Garden Room extension, with the Reform UK-controlled council stating the space would become "a flexible space for exhibitions, art workshops, and more".

The council said Prelude features work by six local artists "each with their own individual style".

Work by Charlotte Ashman, Samantha Brockway, Serena Durgheu, Rosie Jarvis, Simon Loach and Teresa Williams will be on show, with the council saying it would "bring painting, printmaking, collage and photography together in one space".

Greg Wilcox, the council's Reform UK executive member for communities, said: "This is an exciting moment for the team at the Alfred East Gallery, as well as residents.

"It will be great to see the site being used as it has always been intended – showcasing beautiful art."

Work to repair the Grade II-listed building has cost £4.8m, though was initially earmarked for a budget of up to £6.8m.

The Alfred East Art Gallery is named after Sir Alfred East, a famous landscape painter born in Kettering.

He was knighted in 1910 and served as president of the Royal Society of British Artists before his death in 1913.

articles.title: A small Scottish town raised Â£6 million to buy 10,500 acres from a major landowner; its new nature reserve is now restoring 190 hectares of degraded peatland
articles.summary: UK News: When people in the small Scottish town of Langholm set out to raise Â£6 million, they were not simply trying to buy a piece of countryside. Their campa.
articles.body: When people in the small Scottish town of Langholm set out to raise Â£6 million, they were not simply trying to buy a piece of countryside. Their campaign secured 10,500 acres and helped create the community-owned Tarras Valley Nature Reserve, turning an ambitious local vision into one of the region's largest community-led conservation efforts. Now, that decision is shaping how the landscape is managed. According to Tarras Valley Nature Reserve, more than 190 hectares of degraded peatland at Middlemoss Head are being restored, with work focused on repairing damage that has left parts of the bog dry and vulnerable to erosion.More than 54 kilometres of artificial drains are being blocked, while exposed peat is being repaired to help water return to the landscape. As the ground becomes wetter again, the project aims to create conditions where wading birds, insects and rare plants can return and thrive. For Langholm, the restoration is a chance to turn its remarkable land purchase into lasting environmental change.Peatland restoration targets 54 kilometres of drains across Middlemoss HeadThe Langholm Initiative developed the restoration programme with the Crichton Carbon Centre, a Dumfries and Galloway-based peatland specialist, through Scotland's National Peatland Action Programme. The aim is not simply to protect what remains, but to reverse some of the damage caused to the peatland over time.Peatlands are particularly valuable because healthy bogs hold water and store carbon. When they dry out, exposed peat can erode and the landscape becomes less capable of supporting the plants and wildlife associated with functioning bog habitats.At Middlemoss Head, the restoration work is designed to change that. More than 54 kilometres of artificial moorland drains are being blocked to raise water levels and help the dried peatland move back towards a wetter, bog-like state. Areas where peat has become exposed will also be restored to reduce further erosion.Blocked drains help restore wetlands and support rare speciesThe changes may look fairly simple on the ground: drainage channels blocked, damaged peat repaired and water allowed to remain in the landscape.But the intention is to create a patchwork of healthier habitats capable of supporting a much wider range of life. The reserve expects the restored areas to benefit wading birds, insects and rare plants as the peatland recovers.The first phase has already shown signs of what that could mean. Peatland ACTION reported in April 2025 that hundreds of small wetland pools had appeared across the restored area after more than 54 kilometres of drains were blocked.The restoration has also involved removing self-seeded, regenerating Sitka spruce from parts of the site, while specialist low-ground-pressure machinery was used to carry out the work without placing unnecessary pressure on the fragile ground.What started as a land campaign is now helping restore peatlandThe restoration is part of the reason the community fought so hard to take ownership of the land in the first place.The campaign began after Buccleuch Estates announced in 2019 that it planned to sell 25,000 acres of Langholm Moor and the Tarras Valley. Local people rallied behind an ambitious idea: rather than see the landscape pass to another owner, they would try to buy part of it themselves and turn it into a nature reserve.The fundraising became known locally as the âimpossible dreamâ. A major public campaign eventually enabled the community to acquire land in stages, with the wider effort ultimately securing 10,500 acres.Peatland restoration was one of the ambitions behind that campaign. The reserve was intended to bring together nature recovery, climate action and community regeneration rather than treat them as separate goals.That makes the work at Middlemoss Head more than a conventional conservation project. The people who helped secure the land are now seeing one of the original promises of the buyout take shape on the ground.Restoring a landscape the community now controlsFunding for the capital works has come with support from SP Transmission through its Biodiversity Enhancement Strategy. The company has set targets around biodiversity, including achieving no net loss by 2028 and becoming nature positive by 2030.For Langholm, however, the significance reaches beyond those corporate targets. The community takeover transformed the relationship between the town and its surrounding landscape. Land that had once been part of a large private estate is now being managed with nature recovery and local involvement at its centre.The restoration programme is also not intended to be a one-off intervention. The reserve has been developing longer-term plans for additional peatland restoration, with the aim of blocking many more drainage channels across the valley. What started with a fundraising campaign and an ambitious decision to buy thousands of acres has therefore entered a different phase. The challenge now is to give the land time to recover.For Langholm, that means the Â£6 million community buyout is becoming something tangible: not just land held in local hands, but a landscape being actively repaired for the wildlife and people who depend on it.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Europe’s gas prices are surging. Who will be the first to pay more?
articles.summary: Europe could face its toughest winter gas season since 2022 as wholesale prices trade near their highest level in more than three years. Household bills coul...
articles.body:
Gas and electricity bills could increase in Europe this winter if wholesale prices remain elevated long enough to feed through to consumers.

The benchmark European wholesale natural gas price, the Dutch front-month TTF, was trading at over €66 per megawatt-hour (MWh) later on Tuesday, down from above €68 earlier in the session. This compares with around €29/MWh at the beginning of the year.

The rally has been fuelled by growing investor concerns that the Strait of Hormuz could remain closed into the winter.

This comes at a time when the EU's gas-storage levels remain historically low ahead of the heating season.

EU gas storage was 62.99% full at the end of the gas day on 24 August, according to data from Gas Infrastructure Europe.

"Europe's gas stores are unusually low for the time of year," Natasha Fielding, editorial manager for gas, LNG, coal and biomass at Argus Media, told Euronews Business. She added that this level was far below the five-year average of 79%.

"The only other time in the last 15 years that stocks were close to as low was in 2021, ahead of the last major gas crisis," Fielding said.

Among the larger European markets with the lowest storage levels, Germany's stores were only 51% full, while those in the Netherlands stood at 44.3%.

Oxford Economics pointed out in a report published on 13 August — before the latest icrease in gas prices — that EU gas consumption is around 15%-20% lower than in 2021.

It said the EU can operate with lower storage levels, although that would mean relying on more winter LNG imports. And that could leave the EU more exposed to competition with Asian buyers for available cargoes.

The competition is already intensified due to the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz, disrupting a route that normally carries almost one-fifth of global LNG trade.

In a potential EU-Asia bidding war, wholesale prices could climb further.

At current levels, prices "will not be enough for Europe to manage storage through winter," Goldman Sachs analysts Samantha Dart and Laura Cyr wrote in a note cited by Bloomberg.

"In a scenario where Middle East energy exports normalise only gradually through 2027, we estimate that December 2026 TTF would likely need to move above €100/MWh," they said. That is 110% above Goldman's €50/MWh base case, they added.

Oxford Economics said the EU might be forced to suspend parts of its ban on Russian gas imports if supplies tightened further. According to the latest European Commission calculation, Russia's share of combined pipeline and LNG imports was around 12.5% in 2025.

articles.title: Dorset and Hampshire 1976 heatwave was 'like a war zone'
articles.summary: As another hot summer prompts comparisons with 1976, people say the memories remain vivid.
articles.body:
People who lived through the heatwave of 1976 have said memories of the flames, intense heat and fear remain as vivid today as they were 50 years ago.

Dorset and Hampshire residents, firefighters and police officers recalled fast-moving blazes that threatened a fuel depot, forced a hospital evacuation and left communities on edge.

The 1976 heatwave saw 15 consecutive days of temperatures exceeding 32C, and comparisons have been made between the UK's recent high temperatures and the heatwave 50 years ago.

Many said they could still remember sleepless nights, the smell of smoke and uncertainty over what might happen next.

Former retained firefighter Mike Briggs said: "It was just like a war zone. It was so intense, you couldn't fight it."

At one point a fire approached St Leonards Hospital near Ringwood in Dorset.

Former police officer Graham Walbrin said evacuating the hospital was an unprecedented step.

"It was totally unheard of, the fact you evacuate the hospital with elderly people and beds and everything else," he said.

"The trauma for the patients being turfed out of their beds and moved out in the middle of the road."

The scale of the danger became clear when flames approached West Moors and a major nearby fuel depot.

Geoff, who was 11 at the time, said: "I remember the BBC national news, it was the headline article saying something like fire threatens NATO's largest petroleum dump in Europe.

He recalled people being told to leave their homes as crews raced to protect the site.

Briggs said firefighters eventually had to force their way inside.

"We just got in there and it [the fire] was licking around the tanks with thousands of gallons of fuel," he said.

Another firefighter remembered fearing the consequences if the tanks had not been full and had vapour in them that could ignite.

"Thankfully, they were full," he said. "But I was glad to leave that site that day."

Within the past month wildfires have scorched southern England.

According to Reading University's Atmospheric Observatory, by mid-July, more days had reached at least 30C in the summer than in 1976, which was previously the benchmark for hot summers.

It said five of this year's 15 days were in the top 20 highest temperatures ever recorded at the university since it started collecting data in 1908.

Prof Andrew Charlton-Perez, from the university, said: "For half a century, 1976 was the benchmark every hot summer got measured against. Now 2026 has taken its place."

Half a century on, those who lived through the summer of 1976 said the memories had never really faded.

"It doesn't seem 50 years ago because you remember it quite vividly," said resident Ian Knight.

"It was a scary time for people that remember it back in '76.

"A lot of people were genuinely frightened, you know, to go to bed at night."

And Knight said the smell lingered long after the flames had been extinguished.

"We were told, keep your windows shut. The smell of the fire just lingered for weeks."

Months of hot, dry weather helped create conditions for a series of major fires, stretching emergency services and threatening communities across Dorset and Hampshire.

Briggs recalled facing flames that were impossible to control.

"It was just a wall of flame," he said. "It was crowning in the tops of the trees."

As crews battled multiple blazes, local people were asked to help, and Knight said police approached him and his friends to assist firefighters.

"They said, 'Have you got any spare time?'" he recalled. "'The fire brigade are really stretched'."

The group were handed fire beaters and spent hours helping tackle small outbreaks.

The effects were felt by firefighters' families too.

Dawn, whose husband Dave was among those tackling the blazes, said: "All the bedding stank, everything.

"Although he showered, it still smelt. It was absolutely awful. It was just non-stop, every single day," she added.

articles.title: Muck-spreading: The smellier the better as farmers ask for patience
articles.summary: East Yorkshire farmers explain the process as they prepare their fields for next year's crops.
articles.body:
Farmers are asking people to be patient with the smell of manure as they spread it on their fields to prepare the land for next year's crops.

Muck-spreading is the process of distributing animal manure across farmland as a natural fertiliser and typically takes place twice a year, in spring and late summer.

Although "it might smell a bit", according to farmer Ben Clappison, from Cowlam, East Yorkshire, he says it is important as it helps improve the land and reduces the amount of chemical fertilisers.

He says: "[It helps] to make everything a lot healthier and improve soil organic matter and really push towards more organic fertilisers rather than inorganic."

Ben adds: "Our inorganics are manufactured fertilisers and a lot of raw products come from abroad. There's a lot of mileage on it, a lot of CO2 emitted in manufacturing it and it's expensive. Whereas this is coming out of the farm where it's produced."

Ben, who also spreads on other farmland as a contractor, says the process is carefully mapped out using the latest technology.

Manure from cattle, pigs and poultry is scooped from heaps in the fields and carefully weighed to be spread evenly.

Ben also uses human waste, known as sludge and taken from sewage works, to enrich the soil.

However, there are strict rules that farmers must follow when spreading sludge and Ben says he uses GPS to ensure it is only placed in the correct areas.

According to DEFRA, it can only be spread on crops that cannot be eaten directly from the land, such as wheat, barley and oil seed rape.

"We have a spreading app which has everything mapped out and all of the buffer zones and strips where you can't go anywhere near.

"We have to look after the fields, the soils, the environment because it has to be sustainable for not just my generation but generations to come."

The process can generate complaints from residents because of strong odours, although farmers say the smell is short-lived and an unavoidable part of food production.

Those unhappy with the smell can complain to the Environment Agency or their local authority.

However, as a rule, East Riding of Yorkshire Council says it is only likely to investigate if the smell is "particularly excessive or prolonged", adding "spreading manure on farmland is recognised as standard agricultural practice and odour can be expected from time to time".

The process, which takes place after a harvest, is seen as the first step in preparing the land for the next crop.

Angela Kirkwood, of the National Farmers' Union, says a strong smell is a sign of healthy soil.

"What we're trying to do is make the weeds grow so that we can get rid of those weeds but also incorporate that nutrient back into the soils to make the soil really good and healthy.

"We have a lot of soil testing that we do in order to look at what nutrients are already there and how we can improve the nutrients to make our crops grow and to make sure that we can continue producing food for everybody," she says.

"People just think of it as being a stinky process. And all farmers live it as well. Actually, the stinkier the muck, the better it is for the soil."

Angela advises residents to close their windows if they see muck-spreading taking place and not to put any washing out.

Although the smell cannot be helped, farmers say they do understand the complaints.

On Sunk Island in rural Holderness, arable farmer Jono Dixon says he is careful to reduce the impact of spreading chicken muck on his land near Patrington Haven Leisure Park.

He says: "We have the anxiety of spreading it because we know we're going to get the odd complaint, here there and everywhere, or from everybody.

"But this is a quick operation. We've seen in the other field, over there, where within 12 hours the lads are in behind ploughing all the chicken manure in.

"We are trying to do the best we can to not inconvenience people with what can be described as one hell of an odour."
